title: Developer Runbook & System Guide
subtitle: A beginner-friendly guide to how our app runs, how to deploy, and what to do when things go wrong.

topics.title: Where does traffic go?
topics.content: Users connect to https://api.ufitgo.ng. This goes to an AWS Load Balancer (a traffic cop) which looks at the URL (like /api/user or /api/payment) and forwards the request to the correct backend service. Our backend code runs on AWS ECS (Elastic Container Service) using Fargate, which automatically manages the servers for us.
topics.resolution: Rule of thumb: Never point our domain directly to a single server's IP address. The Load Balancer should handle all incoming traffic.

topics.title: Our Backend Services
topics.content:
We have several independent backend services running:
• Admin API (Port 3002)
• Advisor API (Port 3005)
• Operator API (Port 3001)
• Payment Service (Port 8888)
• User API (handles users, wallets, savings, KYC) (Port 3000)
• Notification Service (emails, push notifications) (Port 8001)

AWS ECS automatically starts these services and connects them to the Load Balancer.
topics.resolution: If a service is down, check the AWS ECS dashboard first to see if the service is running successfully before digging into the code.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code
topics.content: We define all our AWS servers and settings using code (CloudFormation files located in backend/aws/cloudformation/), rather than clicking around the AWS dashboard. This means we have a history of changes.
topics.resolution: Always update the CloudFormation files when changing infrastructure. If you make a quick fix in the AWS console, make sure to update the code files too, otherwise your fix will get overwritten on the next deployment.

topics.title: Databases and Secrets
topics.content:
We use PostgreSQL as our main database and Redis for caching. Important rule: Services are not allowed to read each other's databases directly. They must communicate through APIs.

Passwords and API keys (secrets) are securely stored in AWS Parameter Store, not in the code.
topics.resolution: Never paste passwords or secret keys in tickets, Slack, logs, or code. Always use AWS Parameter Store to manage them.

topics.title: Public Routes
topics.content:
The Load Balancer uses simple rules to send traffic to the right place:
• /api/admin/* goes to Admin
• /api/advisor/* goes to Advisor
• /api/operator/* goes to Operator
• /api/v1/* and /api/payment/* goes to Payment
• Everything else (/api/*) falls back to the User API.
topics.resolution: When adding a new API endpoint, make sure it matches these rules. Be careful not to create rules that conflict with the fallback User API route.

topics.title: Internal Communication
topics.content: Sometimes our services need to talk to each other. They use special /api/internal/ routes. These routes are protected by secret API keys so public users can't access them.
topics.resolution: If you get a '401 Unauthorized' error on an internal route without sending an API key, it means the routing is working correctly! If you get a '404 Not Found', you might have typed the URL wrong.

topics.title: Health Checks
topics.content: The Load Balancer constantly checks if our services are alive by calling specific health URLs (e.g., /api/health). If a service doesn't return a '200 OK' success message, the Load Balancer will stop sending it traffic.
topics.resolution: You can test if a service is healthy by visiting its health URL (like https://api.ufitgo.ng/api/health) in your browser. It should return a success message.

topics.title: Domain Name (DNS)
topics.content: Our domain api.ufitgo.ng is managed by Go54 (https://www.go54.com) and the setup email is betadayfinance@gmail.com login with google SSO. Make sure you have access to this email and Google account for any DNS changes. And the url (api.ufitgo.ng) simply points to our AWS Load Balancer. Having correct DNS settings doesn't guarantee the app is working, it just means people can find the Load Balancer.
topics.resolution: If the app is down, don't change DNS settings unless you are sure the Load Balancer address changed. Usually, it's an app issue, not a DNS issue.

topics.title: How Deployments Work
topics.content: When we push code, GitHub Actions automatically builds a new container image and tells AWS ECS to update. AWS will start the new version, check if it's healthy, and only then turn off the old version (this is called a rolling deployment). This means users experience zero downtime.
topics.resolution: A deployment is only successful if the new version starts up and passes its health checks. Just because the GitHub Action finished building the code doesn't mean it's live yet.

topics.title: What if a deployment fails?
topics.content: If the new code crashes on startup or fails health checks, AWS ECS will automatically stop it and keep the old version running. This safety net is called a 'deployment circuit breaker'.
topics.resolution: If your deployment seems stuck, check the AWS ECS events. It might be failing to start because of a missing environment variable or a database error.

topics.title: How to Rollback manually
topics.content: If a bad version accidentally goes live and you need to revert, you don't need to change DNS or IP addresses. Just go to AWS ECS and update the service to use the previous known-good 'task definition' (version).
topics.resolution: Always record the error logs before rolling back so you can fix the issue later. Never try to manually assign IP addresses to fix a bad deployment.

categories.title: What to do when things break

topics.title: First 5 Minutes of an Outage
topics.content:
Don't panic! Follow these steps:
1. Find out exactly which URL is failing and what the error code is.
2. Check the service's health endpoint to see if it's alive.
3. Check AWS CloudWatch for any 'Zero Healthy Targets' alarms.
4. Check the AWS ECS dashboard to see if the service crashed.
5. Only after confirming the service is actually running should you start digging into the application logs.
topics.resolution: If the error is '503 Service Unavailable' or '504 Gateway Timeout' from AWS, the request didn't even reach our code. Check the Load Balancer and ECS.

topics.title: Understanding CORS Errors
topics.content: If the frontend browser complains about 'CORS' (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), it usually means the backend crashed or the Load Balancer rejected the request before it reached our code. The browser hides the real error and just says CORS.
topics.resolution: CORS is usually a symptom, not the cause. Check if the API is returning 500 errors or is offline entirely before trying to fix CORS settings in the code.

topics.title: Common HTTP Errors
topics.content:
• 200/204: Everything is fine.
• 400/401/403: The request reached our code, but there's a problem with the user's input or they aren't logged in.
• 404: The URL doesn't exist or is pointing to the wrong service.
• 500: Our code crashed.
• 502/503/504: The Load Balancer couldn't talk to our code (service is likely down).
topics.resolution: Always look at the exact error code to know where to start investigating.

topics.title: Alerts and Alarms
topics.content: We have AWS CloudWatch alarms that monitor our services. If a service has zero healthy instances running for more than a minute, it will trigger an alarm and send a notification to our ops team.
topics.resolution: If you get a 'Zero Healthy Targets' alarm, it means the service is completely down. Investigate immediately.

topics.title: Finding Logs
topics.content: All our application logs (console.log, errors) are automatically sent to AWS CloudWatch Logs. Each service has its own log group.
topics.resolution: If a service keeps crashing on startup, check the CloudWatch logs. You might find an error about a missing database connection or a syntax error.

topics.title: Preventing Duplicate Jobs
topics.content:
Because we run multiple copies of our services at the same time, we have to be careful with scheduled background jobs (like sending daily emails). If we aren't careful, every copy of the service will try to send the same email!

To fix this, we use database locks. The first service to grab the lock does the work, and the others skip it.
topics.resolution: If you write a new background job, you MUST use a database lock so it only runs once.

topics.title: Handling Secrets
topics.content:
Our servers run in a private network. They can access the internet, but the outside world can only reach them through the Load Balancer.

Passwords and API keys must be injected into the code using AWS Parameter Store. Don't put sensitive stuff in standard environment variables.
topics.resolution: If a secret key gets leaked, rotate (change) it immediately in AWS Parameter Store and restart the service to pick up the new key.
